en: The leaves of the makahiya plant quickly fold inward when touched to protect themselves from hungry herbivores.
The Philippine tarsier uses its exceptionally long hind legs to leap up to two meters between trees.
Mangrove trees in coastal areas grow specialized aerial roots to absorb oxygen from the air during high tide.
A butterfly undergoes complete metamorphosis, changing from an egg to a larva, then a pupa, before emerging as an adult.
Human skin produces sweat, which evaporates to cool the body down when the internal temperature rises.
The carabao rolls in mud to coat its skin, protecting itself from sunburn and biting insects.
The Philippine jade vine produces long, hanging clusters of bright blue-green flowers to attract bat pollinators.
Decomposer fungi in a forest break down dead fallen leaves, returning essential nutrients back into the soil.
A dog's wet nose helps capture scent chemicals from the air to improve its sense of smell.
Philippine pitcher plants trap and digest insects inside their modified leaves to absorb nutrients from poor soil.
A scab forms over a healing cut to seal the wound and prevent bacteria from entering the body.
Female sea turtles return to the exact same Philippine beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs.
